Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'the people responsible have faced no consequences' is hard to reconcile unless there was a clear perpetrator such as major medical negligence. Nothing else in the profile suggests an interpersonal or negligence-based trauma, so this appraisal appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
issues.explanation: A specific perfume or cologne as a trigger is not impossible, but in the context of life-threatening illness it usually needs some link to a person or setting. Here, the rest of the profile does not support an interpersonal perpetrator or a distinctive sensory cue tied to treatment, making this trigger weakly grounded and less coherent with the other selected items.

vignette: María, a 39‑year‑old European‑American dentist, had long prided herself on the control she seemed to wield over both her patients’ teeth and her own life. On the morning she was diagnosed with a rapidly progressing brain tumor, her calm had been ripped away by a cascade of alarms, a frantic surgery, and a night of searing pain that left her trembling in a sterile operating room. The doctors said it would be a “high‑risk” operation, and as she lay under anesthesia she could feel her body surrendering to the machinery—an experience that would haunt her for years to come. When the post‑operative recovery was over, she emerged from the hospital with a new, invisible weight: the knowledge that a moment of weakness could have cost her life. The hospital’s antiseptic scent has become María’s most immediate trigger. Every time the scent of chlorhexidine lingers in the air of a waiting room or a dental office, she feels a sudden, tightening ache in her chest, as though the room is tightening its grip on her. That same scent is coupled with the image of her own trembling hand during surgery, which fuels a belief that she is a weak person—capable of being overpowered by the very body she once trusted. The memory of the cramped, fluorescent‑lit corridors of the hospital reminds her of the sense of having no options: she could have delayed the surgery, but the risk of the tumor spreading was higher. The fear of having no control resurfaces whenever she sees an old photograph of herself smiling brightly, reminding her that she is no longer the invincible person she used to be. These visceral moments trigger a surge of negative appraisals that María recognizes as her brain’s way of reminding her of the permanent damage she believes she has incurred. The sense that the event has left a lasting scar on her life—both physically and emotionally—fuels the belief that she can no longer trust her own body, because in that moment she was at the mercy of a machine. These negative appraisals, in turn, lead María to adopt maladaptive strategies that keep her from confronting the discomfort that follows. She has learned to avoid looking at her own body, especially in mirrors or in the reflection of a dental chair’s polished metal. Even the simple act of checking her pulse on a blood pressure cuff makes her recoil; the idea that her heart may fail or her brain might misfire terrifies her. In the dental clinic, she keeps patients at a distance, deliberately positioning them so she can see them from the back of the room. She shuns conversation with colleagues, refusing to talk about her illness, convinced that sharing her story would expose her vulnerability and invite judgment. Her avoidance of people and avoidance of talking are both defensive mechanisms that stem directly from her belief that she is weak and that she can no longer trust the world around her. Each time she withdraws, she reinforces the notion that she must remain hidden, as if that would protect her fragile self. The negative appraisals also feed back into María’s perception of triggers. The very idea that she is trapped in a body that cannot be trusted amplifies her experience of entrapment whenever she is surrounded by people or forced into situations that require her to rely on her own physical presence. The sight of her own dental tools, once symbols of precision and competence, now reminds her of the limitations imposed on her by her body. The hospital smell, the old photos, the feeling of having no options—all of these external cues trigger the same appraisal of helplessness, as if her mind has learned to equate those moments with the horror she endured in the operating room. The sense of being trapped by an invisible, unseen force grows each time she experiences a trigger, making her feel more isolated and more convinced that the past has permanently altered her. Conversely, María’s maladaptive strategies keep her negative appraisals alive and intensified. By refusing to talk about her illness, she eliminates the possibility of reframing her experience through dialogue. Each avoidance of discussion or avoidance of physical contact with her own body tightens the knot of self‑destructive beliefs. When she does not confront the reality of her pain or her loss of control, the perception that she is a weak person that can never fully recover only deepens. The cycle of avoidance and belief becomes self‑reinforcing, and María’s once‑thriving dental practice now feels like a stage where she must perform while hiding her most fragile self. It is now three years since the surgery that changed María’s life, and she has watched as the veneer of her competence at the dental office cracks. She no longer feels fully present in the clinic; she is constantly scanning for triggers, for the scent of antiseptic, for the flash of a photo on a break room wall. Her avoidance of people and of speaking about her illness has left her relationship strained and her career stagnant—she has missed several important training opportunities because she feared that a lecture would expose her vulnerability. Her fear of confronting her own body has made her reluctant to even schedule a routine dental check‑up for herself, which she knows is essential for her own health. The decision to seek help came when María found herself unable to finish a simple dental procedure. The patient’s eyes fixed on the gleaming instruments, and the antiseptic smell hit her like a wave; she felt an all‑too familiar wave of panic and the urge to flee. As she stared into the patient’s eye, she realized she could not continue to hide from the truth that she had been living in a self‑imposed prison. She was terrified of losing more of her life to the weight of her beliefs, yet she clung to a fragile hope: that with professional support she might break the cycle and reclaim a sense of agency over her own body and her own narrative.
